title-group.article-title: Anatomic Hip Center Decreases Aseptic Loosening Rates After Total Hip Arthroplasty with Cement in Patients with Crowe Type-II Dysplasia
title-group.subtitle: A Concise Follow-up Report at a Mean of Thirty-six Years*

sec.title: Abstract:
sec.p: We previously reported the two to twenty-two-year results of 145 total hip arthroplasties (THAs) with cement performed from 1969 to 1980 in 117 patients with Crowe type-II dysplasia. The purpose of the present study was to update the long-term effects of a nonanatomic hip center on component loosening and aseptic revision in this cohort. Forty-nine patients (sixty hips) were alive at a mean of thirty-six years. The overall cumulative incidence of aseptic revision at thirty-five years was 32% for acetabular cups and 21% for femoral stems. Acetabular loosening was less likely with a hip center placed within the true acetabular region (TAR), <15 mm superior to the approximate femoral head center (AFHC), <35 mm superior to the interteardrop line (ITL), or within zone 1. Femoral loosening and revision were less likely with the hip center placed <35 mm superior to the ITL and within zone 1. An anatomic hip center was associated with significantly lower loosening and aseptic revision rates for both acetabular and femoral components. The current study supports the placement of acetabular components in an anatomic position to promote long-term durability after THA with cement.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Total hip arthroplasty (THA) is the standard treatment for advanced degenerative arthritis in patients with developmental hip dysplasia. However, acetabular reconstruction in such patients is technically demanding because of anterolateral bone deficiency and increased socket anteversion, which compromise superior coverage. While multiple strategies have been described to address this challenge1-5, the optimal cup position continues to be debated. From a biomechanical standpoint, loads are minimized by placing the hip center as medially, inferiorly, and anteriorly as possible6. However, a high hip center may allow for better bone stock than an anatomic position with some types of dysplasia7.

We previously reported the results at a mean of fourteen years (range, two to twenty-two years) after 145 consecutive primary THAs with cement in 117 patients with Crowe type-II dysplasia8. In that report, we found that superior positioning of the hip center was associated with increased rates of acetabular and femoral component loosening. In the present update to our previous report, we aimed to determine if long-term acetabular and/or femoral component loosening and revision rates were correlated with the initial placement of the hip center relative to superior displacement5, presence within the true acetabular region (TAR)9, and the location as determined with a four-zone system8.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using the Mayo Clinic total joint registry, in which outcomes at five-year intervals are prospectively recorded, we retrospectively reviewed the records on all patients who had undergone THA with cement for Crowe type-II hip dysplasia at our institution from 1969 to 1980. Institutional review board approval was obtained prior to the initiation of the study.

The original series included 145 hips in 117 patients, 82% of whom were female. The mean age was fifty-one years (range, fifteen to seventy-six years) at the time of surgery. Since the previous report, sixty-four patients (eighty hips) died. Prior to these patients’ deaths, twelve hips required both-component revision (ten because of aseptic loosening), two required isolated cup revision because of loosening, and two required isolated stem revision because of loosening. An additional four patients (five hips) were lost to follow-up after a mean of fifteen years (range, two to twenty-two years). The remaining sixty hips in forty-nine living patients were followed for a minimum of thirty years. The mean durations of clinical and radiographic follow-up of the living patients were thirty-six years (range, thirty to forty-three years) and thirty-five years (range, thirty to forty-three years), respectively.

At the time of the initial surgery, all acetabular and femoral components were cemented in place, and no structural autografts or allografts were utilized. The goal of cup placement at our institution during the study period was to create an anatomic hip center. Standard cemented Charnley (Thackray) components were utilized in 100 (69%) of the cases. Miniature Charnley components (Thackray) were used in eleven hips (8%). The remaining implants included T-28 components (Zimmer) in fourteen hips (10%), HD-2 components (Howmedica) in seven, Charnley-Müller components (DePuy) in seven (5%), Aufranc-Turner components (Howmedica) in four (3%), a CAD component (Howmedica) in one (0.7%), and a Peterson-Charnley Mark-III component (Howmedica) in one (0.7%).

Preoperative radiographs were reviewed to confirm that the patients had had Crowe type-II dysplasia prior to surgery10. Initial postoperative radiographs were reviewed to evaluate acetabular component placement. The criteria to assess cup placement included (1) superior displacement of ≥15 or <15 mm from the approximate femoral head center (AFHC)8, (2) superior displacement of ≥35 or <35 mm from the interteardrop line (ITL)5, (3) presence within or outside the true acetabular region (TAR)9, and (4) location as assessed with a four-zone system8 (1 = inferomedial, 2 = superomedial, 3 = superolateral, and 4 = inferolateral) (Fig. 1). All radiographic measurements were corrected for magnification using the known size of the femoral head.

caption.p: The true acetabular region (TAR), as described by Ranawat et al.9, is the area enclosed by an equilateral right triangle (dotted line) with the height and width each equaling 20% of the pelvic height. The inferomedial corner of the TAR is 5 mm lateral to the intersection of the Kohler line with the teardrop. The midpoint of the hypotenuse is the approximate femoral head center (AFHC), which represents the normal hip center. The four-zone system is created by the intersection of a horizontal and a vertical line through a point 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the AFHC8. The dashed line represents the interteardrop line (ITL). The radiograph is reproduced from the article containing the original description of the TAR by Ranawat et al.9.

sec.p: Serial follow-up radiographs were reviewed for all 145 hips. Acetabular components were assessed for lucent lines in the three acetabular zones described by DeLee and Charnley11 on anteroposterior pelvic radiographs, and loosening was classified as described by Hodgkinson et al.12. We considered type-3 and 4 cups to demonstrate radiographic evidence of loosening. Similarly, femoral components were assessed for lucent lines in the seven zones described by Gruen et al.13 on anteroposterior and oblique radiographs, with loosening classified as described by Harris et al.14. Femoral components that were either probably or definitely loose according to their classification were considered loose for the present study.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Given the long-term nature of this study and the high rate of cumulative mortality, a competing risk analysis was utilized to determine the thirty-five-year cumulative incidence of component loosening and revision due to aseptic loosening, with other-cause revision and death considered to be competing risks. When the cumulative incidence with corresponding hazard ratios (HRs) was analyzed according to cup position as a risk factor, it was calculated to thirty years because of the sample size. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the clinical portion of the Mayo hip score15.

sec.title: Acetabular Component Loosening and Revision
sec.p: At the time of the latest follow-up, there had been forty-six acetabular revisions due to aseptic loosening (twenty-eight of which were performed since our previous report8), four due to instability, and one due to infection. The acetabular components were revised at a mean of twenty years (range, four to thirty-one years) following the THA. Twelve living patients had radiographic evidence of loosening of a cup that remained in place. After the performance of competing risk analysis, the thirty-five-year cumulative incidence was 32% (95% confidence interval [CI] = 24% to 40%) for acetabular component revision due to loosening (Fig. 2) and 48% (95% CI = 39% to 56%) for revision for, or radiographic evidence of, acetabular component loosening (Fig. 3). Hips with an anatomic hip center had significantly lower rates of acetabular component loosening and aseptic revision. Acetabular loosening at thirty years was less likely when the hip center had been placed within the TAR (cumulative incidence = 39% [95% CI = 30% to 47%] versus 67% [95% CI = 36% to 83%] for outside the TAR, p = 0.013), <15 mm superior to the AFHC (38% [28% to 46%] versus 74% [44% to 88%] for ≥15 mm, p = 0.001), <35 mm superior to the ITL (35% [26% to 44%] versus 68% [46% to 81%] for ≥35 mm, p = 0.001), or within zone 1 (30% [20% to 39%], p < 0.001) (Table I). Similarly, cup revision due to aseptic loosening was less likely when the hip center had been placed <35 mm superior to the ITL, with a cumulative incidence of 25% (95% CI = 17% to 33%) versus 39% (95% CI = 19% to 54%) at thirty years (p = 0.017) (Table I).

caption.p: The cumulative incidence of acetabular revision due to aseptic loosening at thirty-five years was 32% (95% CI = 24% to 40%).
The cumulative incidence of radiographic or clinical evidence of acetabular loosening at thirty-five years was 48% (95% CI = 39% to 56%).

fn.p: After adjustment for competing risks including death and other-cause revision.
TAR = true acetabular region, AFHC = approximate femoral head center, and ITL = interteardrop line.

sec.title: Femoral Component Loosening and Revision
sec.p: At the time of the latest follow-up, there had been thirty-five femoral stem revisions due to aseptic loosening (ten of which had been performed since our previous report8), three due to instability, two due to fracture, and one due to infection. Femoral revision due to aseptic loosening was performed at a mean of twenty-three years (range, four to thirty-one years) after the original THA. Three living patients had radiographic evidence of loosening of a stem that remained in place. After competing risk analysis was performed, the thirty-five-year cumulative incidence was 21% (95% CI = 14% to 28%) for femoral component revision due to loosening and 23% (95% CI = 16% to 29%) for radiographic evidence of femoral component loosening.

Hips with an anatomic hip center had lower rates of femoral component loosening and aseptic revision. Femoral component loosening at thirty years was less likely when the hip center had been placed <35 mm superior to the ITL (cumulative incidence = 18% [95% CI = 11% to 25%] versus 29% [11% to 43%], p = 0.05) or within zone 1 (17% [9% to 24%], p = 0.021). Similarly, stem revision due to aseptic loosening was less likely when the hip center had been placed <35 mm superior to the ITL (cumulative incidence =15% [95% CI = 8% to 22%] versus 26% [9% to 40%], p = 0.025) or within zone 1 (14% [7% to 21%], p = 0.039) (Table II).

sec.title: Clinical Outcomes
sec.p: The mean clinical Mayo hip score was 33 points (range, 0 to 70 points) prior to surgery, which had improved to 69 points (range, 13 to 80 points) at the time of our previous report8. At the most recent follow-up, the scores remained significantly improved for the living patients, with a mean score of 58 points (range, 6 to 76 points, p = 0.01).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This thirty-six-year follow-up study of patients who had undergone THA for Crowe type-II dysplasia demonstrated that reconstructions with an anatomic hip center were associated with a lower risk of aseptic loosening and revision of both the acetabular cup and the femoral stem.

The present study had limitations. First, because of its long-term nature, more than half of the patients had died in the interval between the studies, many of them with the original components in place. While we did adjust our cumulative incidence estimates for competing risks, including death and other-cause revision, our results should be interpreted in light of this fact. Furthermore, radiographic analysis of loosening is an imperfect science with limitations in interobserver and intraobserver variability. Finally, cemented components are not commonly used in contemporary THA, particularly on the acetabular side, and these findings are not necessarily predictive of the outcomes of cementless fixation.

Johnston et al.6 showed that hip centers placed inferiorly, medially, and anteriorly should theoretically experience lower reaction forces and biomechanical stress. Their mathematical model provides theoretical support for the lower loosening and revision rates for anatomic relative to nonanatomic hip centers demonstrated in several subsequent clinical series8,9,16. Our findings are in accordance with these prior reports. When applying these results to contemporary practice, it is important to note that these studies were of cemented components.

The argument for a high hip center is that it potentially provides improved component coverage and more robust bone stock. Interestingly, recent reports have shown excellent outcomes in dysplastic hips treated with a superiorly placed cementless acetabular component. Kaneuji et al.17 found that twenty-nine hips treated with a cementless cup placed a mean of 26.8 mm superior to the ITL had a 100% survival rate free of loosening at a mean of fifteen years. Similarly, Murayama et al.18 reported 97% survivorship at a mean of fifteen years after treatment of thirty-three hips with a cementless cup placed a mean of 24.5 mm superior to the ITL. Additionally, Nawabi et al.19 reported no cases of aseptic loosening at ten to twenty years in thirteen hips with Crowe type-II dysplasia in which a cementless cup had been placed a mean of 24.6 mm superior to the ITL. In each of these reports, the authors concluded that slight superior placement of the uncemented acetabular component led to excellent results.

While the positive results of nonanatomically placed uncemented components are intriguing, such reports must be interpreted with attention to the definition of a “high hip center.” In the three aforementioned studies of uncemented components, the hip center was placed an average of 24 to 27 mm superior to the interteardrop line. These mean values would actually be classified as “anatomic” if the methods used in our study were applied. While it is conceivable that anatomic cup placement may be less crucial in the setting of biologic fixation, longer follow-up and more thorough attention to the definition of the hip center will be necessary in the future. As cemented acetabular components are now rarely used at our institution, our current practice for patients with Crowe type II dysplasia is to accept slightly superior cup placement when performing cementless THA.

In summary, acetabular reconstruction in patients with dysplasia of the hip remains a challenge. While options are often dictated by the degree of dysplasia and the specific extent and location of bone loss in an individual patient, the current study supports the contention that placement of acetabular components in an anatomic position promotes long-term durability of both the acetabular and the femoral component after THA with cement.
